freshness.notes: The RSS feed, used as a change signal and NOT as the content. Measured 2026-08-24: it held 3 items while the listing held 89 across ten paginated pages, so building the artifact from it would silently drop the most consequential closure (features/ATC_TRAIL_UPDATES.md, 'what the feed does not carry'). The 2026-08-09 version of this note read '3 items while the page showed 9'; the 9 was page one mistaken for the whole list, which is https://github.com/OurHike/OurHike/issues/945. It does carry an ETag that moves when ATC edits, which is all a freshness marker needs - WEAK (`W/"..."`) as measured 2026-08-24, where this note said 'strong' on 2026-08-12; check_freshness.py compares it verbatim and only asks whether it moved, but a weak validator lets the upstream change the bytes without changing the tag. The listing page itself is still not usable as the marker, and now for two reasons. The correction this note carried briefly on 2026-08-24 - 'it no longer 403s a scripted request, it answers 200' - was measured with curl and did not describe the pipeline's own client: re-measured the same day, ATC refuses the literal `python-requests/*` User-Agent with 403 and answers 200 to curl and to a named agent, so the original 2026-08-12 finding was right about check_freshness.py and still is. lib/atc_scrape.py reaches the listing only because it sets a User-Agent naming the project. On top of that, a HEAD on the listing returns neither an ETag nor a Last-Modified, so even an allowed request would give a marker of UNKNOWN forever.

sources.notes: 8,823 point features statewide, measured 2026-08-18. The layer's own display name is 'NY State Parks Facilities (Internal)' although the service is public - what that naming implies about the schema's intended audience is unassessed. dataLastEditDate verified live 2026-08-18 (then 2026-08-12). IT CARRIES WATER, measured live 2026-08-27 and answering the question #769 and NYC_SOURCE_SURVEY.md §10(g) left open: `Sub_Asset` has 158 distinct values, among them **136 'Water Spigot' and 15 'Drinking Fountain'** (plus 'Mineral Spring', 'Water Tower' and 'Waterfall', which are not drinking water and must not be read as such). So the evidence bar CLAUDE.md's four ways sets is now live for this layer rather than hypothetical - shipping it is a water change, and needs export_poi.py's confidence and provenance treatment the way `osm_water` got one, not a plain point dump. `Asset` is a coded integer 1-17 whose domain the service does NOT publish, so the type of a facility is only readable through `Sub_Asset`'s free text; that is the join hazard to solve before any of these become waypoints. HOW THAT RESOLVED: the layer ships as of 2026-08-27 (#1097) via export_nearby_poi.py, which reads the type through `Sub_Asset`'s free text as this note said it would have to, and `reaches_hikers` is true for that reason. The water is the one part held back, and the sentence above about the evidence bar is why - see oprhp_water_holdback for the two questions that have to be answered before a spigot becomes a pin. An earlier version of this note ended '`reaches_hikers` stays false because nothing exports this layer'; that was true when written and survived the export being wired, which is the failure it is now recorded against.
sources.public_field_comment: NOT `Public_`, which reads Y on all 8,823 rows and therefore discriminates nothing (measured 2026-08-27). ParksApp is the field that does, 5,822 Y / 3,000 N - but it records what OPRHP's own visitor app SHOWS rather than what exists on the ground, so it SETS CONFIDENCE rather than filtering: dropping its N side would discard every one of OPRHP's 37 lean-tos, none of which are in that app. An N row ships at CONFIDENCE_LOW, which the map draws with a broken rim and the legend's 'Verified?' filter removes. This is the opposite reading from DEC's PUBLICUSE and the difference is measured, not stylistic - see export_nearby_poi.py's docstring and POI_COVERAGE_SURVEY.md §2.
sources.id_field_comment: Declared rather than left to export_nearby_poi.py's `OBJECTID` default, which is what this entry did until now - alone among the six POI layers, every DEC one of which declares it. The default gave the right answer, so nothing was wrong on the ground; what was wrong is that the registry did not RECORD the join, and a reader comparing this entry against DEC's could only conclude the layer had no stable id. It does: the service's own `objectIdField` and `uniqueIdField` both read OBJECTID, verified live 2026-08-28.
sources.name_field_comment: `Name` is populated on 1,631 of 8,823 rows (18%, measured 2026-08-27) and is flagged '(Legacy Field)' in the layer's own alias. The other 82% export with no name and the client renders them 'Unnamed', which is the honest outcome: `Facility` (populated on all 8,823) is the PARK's name, not the feature's, and publishing 'Beaver Island State Park' as the name of a bridge inside it would be a different fact than the one a hiker reads. It goes into the composed description instead - export_nearby_poi.py's compose_description, which is lib/poi_description.py's idea applied to another org's columns.

sources.foot_allowed_comment: WHAT `M` IN THE FOOT COLUMN IS READ AS, because dec_hiking_trails' foot_allowed keeps those 1,236 rows and the reading is ours rather than DEC's. DEC's CORRIDOR USE domain declares five codes with these labels, read off the live field metadata 2026-08-25: Y=YES, N=NO, U=UNDECIDED, M=MAINTAINED, -99=NO JURISDICTION. `M` is read here as 'DEC maintains this corridor for foot travel', which is at least as strong a statement about walkability as Y. @unvalidated - DEC publishes no data dictionary this project has found that defines the code per row, so the reading rests on the domain's own label plus what the rows look like: measured 2026-08-25, 991 of the 1,236 M rows are ASSET 'FOOT TRAIL', 681 carry a trail-marker colour, and the named ones are ordinary hiking trails (Bog Meadow Trail, the Finger Lakes Trail, the North Country Trail, the Long Path). What would settle it: DEC's own documentation of the CORRIDOR USE matrix, or the same conversation open_question above names. What the alternative costs: a foot_allowed of ['Y'] alone drops 23% of the layer DEC itself publishes as hiking trails, including named through-trails - a hiking-only filter deleting hiking trails, which is the wrong way for this to fail.

sources.notes: 5,286 polyline segments (4,931 LineString, 355 MultiLineString), fetched whole and counted 2026-08-25 - against the 5,277 NYC_SOURCE_SURVEY.md §3 read on 2026-08-11, so the layer moves. Fields UNIT/FACILITY/NAME/ASSET/MILES/DESCRIP/PUBLICUSE/UPDATED plus the per-use CORRIDOR USE matrix (FOOT/HORSE/BIKE/XC/SNOWMB/ATV/MOTORV/ADMIN/ACCESSIBLE/MAPPWD) and MARKER, which DEC aliases 'Trail Marker Color' and is this pipeline's blaze. FOUR THINGS A READER SHOULD NOT HAVE TO RE-FETCH TO LEARN. (1) MARKER is a genuine coded domain whose codes ARE the words (Red/Yellow/Blue/Orange/Green/White/Other), like oprhp_trails' Blaze and unlike side_trails' integers, so no domain decode stands in front of reference/blaze_mapping.json; live values on the 5,286 rows are 2,929 blank or null, Yellow 704, Blue 692, Red 622, White 128, Other 97, Orange 78, Green 35, and one 'ORANGE AND RED' that DEC's own domain does not declare. (2) FOOT reads Y on 4,050 rows and M on 1,236, and nothing else - see foot_allowed and foot_allowed_comment above. (3) THERE IS NO STATUS COLUMN, so every kept row exports as open under export_nearby_trails.py's DEFAULT_STATUS: DEC publishes no closure state here, and inventing one would be the failure that module's closure treatment exists to avoid. PUBLICUSE reads 'Y' on all 5,286, which is a layer-wide constant rather than a filter worth having. (4) IDS FALL BACK TO OBJECTID, because DEC spells the column GLOBALID and lib/feature_id.py looks for GlobalID - the ids are unique across the fetched 5,286 and stable within a fetch, but a DEC republish that renumbers OBJECTIDs would renumber ours; the stable column is there for the taking if that ever bites. THE LAYER'S OWN SCOPE, stated because the name oversells it: 'Hiking Trails' is DEC's per-use split, so a row is here because foot travel is allowed on it, not because it is a footpath - 446 rows are ASSET 'SNOWMOBILE TRAIL' with FOOT 'Y', 456 are unpaved roads, and they are walkable corridors on DEC land rather than mistakes. PUBLICUSE splits the layer 7,645 Y / 13,823 N and is the only reason this layer is publishable at all. sources.national_trail_designation_comment: @unvalidated, BUT MUCH BETTER EVIDENCED THAN WHEN THIS ENTRY WAS FIRST WRITTEN - and the change is a correction of this note's own over-caution, recorded rather than swapped. national_trail_designation is an integer whose `domain` reads null on the live field metadata (2026-09-02), so the Forest Service publishes no decode. FILTER', on the strength of GREAT GULF and MADISON GULF carrying it. AN INDEPENDENT SOURCE NOW SAYS OTHERWISE. nh_granit_trails covers the same ground from a different publisher, and its white-blazed set - 62 rows, 61 of them TRAILSYS 'Appalachian Trail' - names essentially the same trails code 3 does: Beaver Brook, Benton, Carter-Moriah, Cascade Brook, Centennial, Crawford Path, Ethan Pond, Fishin' Jimmy, Franconia Ridge, Garfield Ridge, Glencliff, Gulfside, Kenduskeag, Kinsman Ridge, Liberty Spring - AND GREAT GULF AMONG THEM. So the row that was this note's main counter-example is grouped with the A.T. by BOTH publishers independently, which makes it far likelier that code 3 means the Appalachian National Scenic Trail and that Great Gulf is a corridor/adjacency call the two agencies happen to share, than that two unrelated sources made the same mistake. CRAWFORD PATH also still splits across codes 1, 2 AND 3, which no 'code 3 = the A.T.' reading explains. What would settle it: the Forest Service's data dictionary for the TrailNFS publish schema. What to do meanwhile: do not route on it. A hiker's A.T. route comes from ATC's own centerline, which this pipeline already ships and which is authoritative for exactly this question.

sources.foot_allowed_comment: WHY trail_type IS THE foot_field HERE, when on other sources that slot holds an actual foot column. export_nearby_trails.py's foot_field/foot_allowed pair means 'the field that decides whether you can walk this, and the values that say yes'. For OPRHP and DEC that is a per-use foot column. USFS publishes its trails split by MEDIUM instead: measured nationwide 2026-09-02, trail_type reads TERRA on 78,101 rows, SNOW on 8,152 and WATER on 76. The 8,228 non-TERRA rows are snowmobile and paddle corridors - a first page of WMNF results is HIX MTN RD SNOMO, BERRY FARM SNOMO, ROSEBROOK SNOMO - so TERRA is exactly the walkable set and the drop reason this prints ('not a foot trail: trail_type=SNOW') is true as written. WHY NOT hiker_pedestrian_managed, WHICH IS THE OBVIOUS CANDIDATE AND IS A TRAP. It is a SEASON STRING ('01/01-12/31'), not a flag, so it cannot be an allowed-set at all - and it is NULL on 35,667 of the 78,101 TERRA rows. Requiring it would delete 46% of the Forest Service's terrestrial trail inventory. Absent is unrecorded, not prohibited, which is the same lesson dec_hiking_trails' foot_allowed_comment records for DEC's `M` and nh_granit_trails' foot_comment records for GRANIT's blank PED - three sources, three vocabularies, one mistake. AND THE LAYER ESSENTIALLY NEVER PROHIBITS FOOT TRAVEL: 78,064 of the 78,101 TERRA rows carry at least one populated hiker_pedestrian_* column, and hiker_pedestrian_restricted reads the literal string 'N/A' on 399 of a 400-row sample of the rows where it is set. So there is no prohibition signal to honour even if one were wanted. WHAT IS LEFT UNDONE, said rather than guessed: the four-column per-use matrix (managed/accpt/disc/restricted x fifteen uses) is undecoded, so this export cannot yet tell a trail MANAGED for hikers from one where hiking is merely accepted, and it cannot exclude a bike or OHV trail that also allows foot travel. That is a real gap against the maintainer's 'It's OurHike, not OurBike' rule - it keeps corridors a stricter reading would drop - and it wants the Forest Service's data dictionary rather than a guess at their column semantics.
sources.blaze_default_comment: THE FOREST SERVICE PUBLISHES NO BLAZE COLUMN AT ALL - not a blank one, none - across the 100-odd fields of the TrailNFS publish schema, checked against the live field list 2026-09-02. So this states the absence rather than asserting a paint, exactly as nynjtc_highlands_trail's blaze_default does for the same reason. IT IS 'Unknown' AND NOT 'None', AND THE DIFFERENCE IS THE POINT: 'None' means a CONFIRMED unblazed trail (the client renders it 'Unblazed'), which is what nh_granit_trails' blank BLAZE earns because GRANIT does record blazes where they exist and records none here. USFS records nothing either way, so the honest word is 'Blaze not recorded'. Two sources covering the same White Mountains ground, two different absences, and collapsing them would tell a hiker the Forest Service had checked. It also has a mechanical job: network_line_sources() identifies a trail-LINE source by the presence of blaze_field or blaze_default, so without this key export_nearby_trails.py would skip this layer entirely as if it were a points layer - which it did, until a test caught it.

sources.blaze_comment: BLANK IS NOT A GAP HERE - IT IS THE GROUND. This entry carried the opposite reading for a few hours on 2026-09-02 and it was wrong, so the correction is written down rather than quietly swapped: the first version registered WITHOUT a blaze_field, on the argument that BLAZE is blank on 7,574 of the 7,643 Whites rows (99.1%) and that painting from a 0.9%-populated column would draw the region as a data outage. THE MAINTAINER CORRECTED IT THE SAME DAY, from knowing the ground: the White Mountains largely do not use paint blazes. AMC's convention there is cairns above treeline and unmarked tread below, so a Whites trail having no blaze is the normal case and GRANIT recording none is GRANIT being right. THE DATA CONFIRMS THE CORRECTION, measured 2026-09-02 and worth keeping because it turns a domain fact into a checkable one: of the 62 rows that DO read White, 61 carry TRAILSYS 'Appalachian Trail' and their names are the A.T.'s own route through the Whites - Beaver Brook, Kinsman Ridge, Franconia Ridge, Garfield Ridge, Ethan Pond, Crawford Path, Gulfside, Carter-Moriah, Glencliff, Liberty Spring, Centennial. The 62nd is Lost Pond Trail (TRAILSYS 'Square Ledge'), which runs beside the A.T. at Pinkham Notch. The only other blazes in the whole bbox are 4 Yellow, 2 Red and 1 Blue, every one of them in a lowland wildlife sanctuary or conservation easement (Dahl Wildlife Sanctuary, Burleigh CE, Red Hill) rather than in the mountains. So the column is not sparse - it is CORRECT: the A.T. is white-blazed through the Whites and almost nothing else up there is blazed at all, and that is exactly the picture GRANIT publishes. WHAT THIS MEANS FOR THE MAP: a blank must render as 'no blaze', which is a true statement about a Whites trail, and never as 'unknown'. The one thing still unstated is GRANIT's own semantics - they do not document whether blank means 'unblazed' or 'not recorded', and the reading that it means unblazed rests on the maintainer's knowledge of the region plus the A.T. correlation above, not on anything GRANIT says. That is a sound basis and it is not the publisher's word, which is the distinction this note exists to keep visible.
sources.foot_comment: WHY NO foot_field, AND WHY 'PED' IS THE WRONG ONE. GRANIT publishes a per-use matrix (PED/MTNBIKE/XCSKI/SNOWMBL/ATV/HORSE/...), so PED looks like oprhp_trails' Foot and dec_hiking_trails' FOOT. It is not, and export_nearby_trails.py's allowed-set mechanism would misread it. Measured 2026-09-02 across the 7,643 Whites rows: PED reads '1' on 3,883 and BLANK on 3,760, and blank means UNRECORDED rather than no. Of those 3,760 blanks, 2,541 carry NO use flag of any kind - not snowmobile, not ATV, not bike, not ski, not horse - and their names are ordinary hiking trails (Alpina Trail, Bathtub Trail, Beaver Pond Trail), one of them literally 'Appalachian Trail - road link'. A foot_allowed of {'1'} would therefore delete 2,541 hiking trails including a piece of the A.T., which is the exact failure dec_hiking_trails' foot_allowed_comment records DEC's {'Y'} would have caused, one state over. WHAT THE LAYER DOES JUSTIFY DROPPING: the 1,209 blank-PED rows flagged SNOWMBL '1' and the 124 flagged ATV '1' are motorized corridors and are not this app's subject. That is a filter on a POSITIVE motorized flag rather than on an absent foot one, and it needs code export_nearby_trails.py does not have today - so nothing is filtered here yet and this comment is the specification for the change that does it.
sources.excluded_when_comment: THE MOTORIZED EXCLUSION, and why it is an exclusion rather than a foot allowlist. foot_comment above shows why foot_field cannot be PED: blank means unrecorded, and 2,541 blank-PED rows in the Whites carry no use flag at all while being ordinary hiking trails. But GRANIT's layer does contain corridors this app has no business drawing as trails - measured 2026-09-02 inside the Whites bbox, 1,209 blank-PED rows are flagged SNOWMBL '1' and 124 are flagged ATV '1'. Those are POSITIVE assertions by GRANIT about what a corridor is for, and acting on a positive assertion is sound where acting on an absence is not. So this drops on the motorized flag and keeps everything else, which is the maintainer's 'It's OurHike, not OurBike' rule applied with the only evidence this layer actually offers. NOT EXCLUDED: MTNBIKE, HORSE and XCSKI, because a mountain-bike or ski trail is walkable ground and dropping it would repeat the deletion this comment exists to avoid.

org_marks._comment: Whether each organization has granted OurHike the right to SHIP ITS MARK, and the answer for every one of them today is no (#933). WHY THIS IS A LICENCE QUESTION AND NOT A DESIGN ONE: OurHike is offline-first, so an org's logo is not fetched when a card renders - it is copied into the download and carried on a hiker's phone, potentially for months, inside an application distributed under AGPL-3.0. That is redistribution, and it needs permission in writing the same way the trail geometry does. A logo is usually held MORE tightly than the data: trademark rather than copyright, with organizations that care a great deal about how their mark is used. WHY THE BLOCK EXISTS WHILE IT IS EMPTY OF GRANTS. The record has to be older than the first asset, or the first asset arrives with the question already forgotten - which is exactly how this repository already ships one trademarked third-party mark whose permission is recorded in a source comment and nowhere else (client/src/lib/trails.ts, the A.T. marker, see the ATC row below). tests/test_org_marks.py is what makes this block bite: it derives the org list from the registry's own providers, so a newly registered organization cannot slip past by not being added to a second place, and it FAILS if a mark asset exists in the client tree for an org whose state here is not `granted`. UNTIL A GRANT ARRIVES, THE SLOT RENDERS EMPTY - never a placeholder mark, never an initial, never a generated shape. An organization's identity is the one thing in this app that must not be approximated, and a visibly empty slot is also the thing most likely to prompt somebody to go and ask.

state_vocabulary.not_asked: Nobody has put the question to this organization. The default, and not a judgement about whether they would say yes.
state_vocabulary.asked: The ask has been sent and no answer has come back. Carries `asked_date` so a silence can be aged rather than forgotten.
state_vocabulary.granted: The organization has given permission in writing. Carries every field in `required_on_grant` below, and is the ONLY state under which a mark asset may exist in the tree.
state_vocabulary.refused: The organization has said no. Recorded rather than deleted, so nobody asks twice and nobody assumes the silence in `not_asked` means this.

permission_meanings.redistribute_in_offline_bundle: The mark may be copied into a downloadable map package and carried on a hiker's phone offline, inside an AGPL-3.0 application. This is the permission that makes the others necessary.
permission_meanings.display_beside_own_attribution: The mark appears beside the organization's own attribution string and never detached from it, so a mark can never read as an endorsement of something the org did not publish.
permission_meanings.no_modification: Not recoloured, not cropped, not composited, not redrawn at a size the org did not supply. `asset` records what they sent; the app renders that.
permission_meanings.brand_colour_chip_only: A brand colour may tint the organization's chip and NOTHING ELSE - above all never a trail line. The map's hue channel means WHICH BLAZE A HIKER FOLLOWS (features/TRAIL_BLAZE_COLORS.md), so an organization's brand colour touching a trail line would make the map say something false about paint on a tree. This is the one permission that is a constraint on OurHike rather than a grant from the org, and it is recorded here because it is the one an implementer is most likely to breach by accident.

reaches_hikers_comment: Why every source entry carries `reaches_hikers` (#927). The sources screen names the organizations whose data is on a hiker's phone, under the terms each one set - so it has to know which registered sources actually SHIP, and that fact lived only in prose inside each entry's `licence` string ('fetched for REVIEW AND CROSS-CHECKS ONLY', 'nothing from this source reaches a published artifact until...'). A screen that decided by reading those sentences would print a licence claim for data nobody publishes the first time one was reworded. So it is a field: true means an exporter reads this source and its data reaches a release, false means registered-but-not-shipped, for any reason - review-only pending a licence answer (gatc_water_sources, every oprhp_*), watched-only (usgs_3dhp), or registered and not yet wired to anything (bridges, at_treadway, per pipeline/README.md). It is NOT a licence judgement and does not replace one: a source can be freely licensed and still not ship. export_sources.py refuses to run if any entry lacks the field, so a newly registered source cannot reach a hiker's screen by defaulting into it.
licence_basis_comment: WHAT A SOURCE'S LICENCE ACTUALLY RESTS ON, as a field rather than as prose (#929). Three values and they are not interchangeable: `stated_by_org` - the organization published terms of its own and they permit this (OPRHP's licenseInfo, ODbL, a federal public-domain work); `maintainer_authorisation` - the organization has stated nothing that reaches this use, and the maintainer authorised it as the person who carries the consequence. IT IS NOT A GRANT FROM THE ORGANIZATION and must never be rendered as one; `unresolved` - nobody has answered, and nothing ships. WHY IT IS A FIELD. Every one of these facts was already written down, in the per-source `licence` prose and the `<x>_licence` blocks - and only there. A screen or a report that wanted to say 'eleven of the thirty-three ship on your own authorisation rather than the org's terms' had to decide it by reading those sentences, which is exactly the failure `reaches_hikers_comment` records for the flag above: 'a screen that decided by reading those sentences would print a licence claim for data nobody publishes the first time one was reworded'. The same argument, one field over. IT IS NOT A JUDGEMENT ABOUT QUALITY and it does not replace the prose: the prose is where the reasoning, the dates, the read terms and the open questions live. This is one word saying which of the three shapes that reasoning has, so it can be counted. Measured 2026-08-27 against this file: 6 stated_by_org, 26 maintainer_authorisation, 1 unresolved.

poi_coverage._comment: What each organization publishes for each of lib/poi_schema.POI_TYPES, and whether OurHike ships it (#1092). The maintainer's ask, 2026-08-27: "We don't have POI for the org's outside of ATC. Search those sources for the POI types we have... Maybe we need to track each of the POI types for the org, and whether or not it is provided." This block is the second half of that - the answer in a form a test can read, so "does DEC give us campsites" stops being a question the next session re-probes from scratch. pipeline/POI_COVERAGE_SURVEY.md is the evidence and the argument; spike_org_poi_coverage.py is the script every count here came from, re-runnable in one command. THE COUNTS ARE OF WHAT THE ORG PUBLISHES, NOT OF WHAT A HIKER WOULD SEE: nothing here is clipped to a corridor, deduped against ATC's POIs, or filtered to walkable ground, because this block is a survey of supply and those are ingest decisions belonging to per-org issues. `org_flags_public` is the subset the org's OWN publication flag marks as visitor-facing - DEC's PUBLICUSE, OPRHP's ParksApp - and it is the more honest of the two numbers wherever the two disagree. Twelve of these cells became `shipping` on 2026-08-27 (#1097, export_nearby_poi.py -> nearby_poi.geojson): six DEC types and six OPRHP ones, 8,480 features. Neither org's water is among them. tests/test_poi_coverage.py enforces that every provider in `sources` has a verdict for every POI type, from the vocabulary below: no blanks, the same discipline NYC_SOURCE_SURVEY.md §9 applies to licensing.

shelter.note: THE FOREST SERVICE PUBLISHES NO TRAIL SHELTER TYPE. The nearest candidate is 815 rows of site_type 'LOOKOUT/CABIN', and a fire lookout or a rentable forest cabin is not what a hiker means by a shelter - it is not open, not free, and in the rental case needs a reservation months out. Shipping those as poi_type shelter would tell a hiker walking into weather that there is a roof ahead they cannot use, which is why this is 'unsuitable' rather than 'available': the data is real and the reading would mislead. What was NOT done, and would be the next step if this mattered: the rows' individual site_name and development_scale values were not examined, so whether any one of them is in fact a backcountry shelter is unknown. Counts are nationwide by group-by statistics on site_type over the layer's 31,405 rows, measured 2026-09-02; the White Mountains subset that prompted the registration is in usfs_rec_sites' notes.

dec_water_holdback: WHY NO WATER SHIPS FROM DEC, recorded beside the sources rather than only in a survey, because the next person to look at dec_backcountry_features will see 'SPRING' and 'WELL' in its ASSET column and reasonably wonder (#1097; the evidence is POI_COVERAGE_SURVEY.md §3, the verdict is poi_coverage.orgs['NYS DEC'].types.water, and tests/test_poi_coverage.py pins it). Measured live 2026-08-27: DEC's only plumbed-water asset type is 'WATER SUPPLY SYSTEM', 23 features, and ZERO of them are flagged PUBLICUSE 'Y' - DEC's own answer is that none of it is for visitors. Sampling 14 found real spigots beside a 'Water Storage Tank', an 'Underground Water Line', and a drilled well whose own NOTES read 'Not Approved For Human Consum[ption]'. The 350 features whose names merely SOUND like water are worse and are also all PUBLICUSE 'N': 207 'WATERHOLE' are fire-and-wildlife impoundments ('Wetland Pool', 'Made by Tioga County SWCD in 2016'), 97 'WELL' are dominated by NATURAL GAS WELLS, 4 'CISTERN' are CCC-era fire cisterns, and 19 'SPRING' include one 'Unnoffical Unsanctioned Traditional Public Wa[ter]' and one 'Untested'. A pipeline matching on the word 'water' would have published 207 fire ponds and 97 gas wells as places to fill a bottle. The maintainer's decision on reading this, 2026-08-27: 'Lets not use water from DEC'. Reopening it should mean NEW DATA FROM DEC - a layer they publish, a flag that flips - and never a new reading of these same 23 rows.
oprhp_water_holdback: WHY OPRHP'S WATER DOES NOT SHIP EITHER, and why its reason is different from DEC's (#1097). OPRHP's water is REAL: 136 'Water Spigot' and 15 'Drinking Fountain' in NY_State_Park_Facilities' Sub_Asset, measured live 2026-08-27, plumbed fixtures named as such - so unlike DEC this is a holdback rather than a refusal, and the poi_coverage verdict stays `available` rather than `unsuitable`. Two things have to be answered first, and neither is answerable from the layer. (1) SEASONALITY IS UNRECORDED. A park spigot is shut off for winter and the layer carries no field saying when; a pin promising water in April where the valve is closed is the failure FEATURES.md names - a confidently wrong prediction is more dangerous than an honest unknown - and water is one of CLAUDE.md's four ways this app can hurt somebody. (2) OPRHP'S OWN APP SHOWS ONLY 15 OF THE 151: every Water Spigot reads ParksApp 'N', so the org itself puts only the drinking fountains in front of visitors, and publishing the other 136 would be going further than the steward does with their own data. Everything else OPRHP publishes ships (shelter, campsite, privy, viewpoint, parking, crossing); this one type waits for an issue of its own with its own evidence, which is the shape export_poi.py's osm_water treatment already sets. Also NOT water and never to be folded in: 'Mineral Spring' (17), 'Water Tower' (12), 'Waterfall' (55).

usfs_licence._comment: The basis on which usfs_trails and usfs_rec_sites may be fetched AND republished to hikers: PUBLIC DOMAIN under 17 U.S.C. 105, adopted by the maintainer on 2026-09-02 ("Move the usfs licence to the public domain"). THIS BLOCK RECORDS A READING OF A STATUTE, NOT A GRANT FROM AN AGENCY, and the difference is the whole reason it is written at length. Section 105 says copyright protection is not available for any work of the United States Government - a work prepared by an officer or employee as part of their official duties. The TrailNFS publish layer and the INFRA recreation-site layer are exactly that, so there is no copyright for the Forest Service to license, withhold, or condition. That is why the licence_basis is `stated_by_org` rather than `maintainer_authorisation`: licence_basis_comment's own vocabulary names 'a federal public-domain work' as an instance of terms that permit this use, and unlike DEC or NYNJTC there is no unanswered ask sitting behind it. THE PATH THIS TOOK, recorded because the file moved twice in one day and a reader deserves to see why rather than a final state that looks obvious. It registered `unresolved` on the morning of 2026-09-02 - the Forest Service states no terms anywhere this survey could read, and the survey declined to settle the statute on their behalf. The maintainer then authorised publication on the grounds that the data is publicly available, which was recorded as `maintainer_authorisation` because public availability is not itself a reuse grant (SOURCE_SURVEY.md's rule, and the rule under which DEC, NYNJTC and Mohonk all sit in that column). The maintainer then made the stronger and more accurate call, which is this one. WHAT WAS ACTUALLY READ FROM THE SERVICES, unchanged by any of that and still worth having: copyrightText is EMPTY at the service level on EDW_TrailNFSPublish_01, read live 2026-09-02; the LAYER carries the bare string 'USDA Forest Service', which is an attribution rather than a grant; EDW_RecreationOpportunities_01 carries a no-warranty disclaimer, which is a disclaimer rather than a grant. Neither service is an AGOL item - both are on-prem ArcGIS - so there is no licenseInfo to quote the way nynjtc_licence and mohonk_licence quote one. NONE OF THAT IS EVIDENCE AGAINST SECTION 105; silence from an agency is what the statute predicts, because there is nothing for them to say. THE LIMITS, which are real and are not licence questions. (1) Section 105 is DOMESTIC: it removes U.S. copyright, and other jurisdictions are not bound by it. (2) It covers works of GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES; a federal agency can hold copyright assigned to it by a contractor, and nothing here has audited these two layers for contributed third-party content. (3) It is not a warranty of accuracy, and the Forest Service's own disclaimer stands - which matters more for a hiker than the licence does. (4) Public domain is not a trademark licence: the Forest Service shield is a mark, is protected separately (18 U.S.C. 711a), and org_marks still reads `not_asked` for USFS. What ships is the DATA. ATTRIBUTION IS KEPT ANYWAY, and is not owed: `attribution` stays 'USDA Forest Service' on both entries because telling a hiker whose survey a line came from is this project's practice regardless of whether a licence compels it.

nh_granit_licence._comment: The basis on which nh_granit_trails may be fetched AND republished to hikers. WHAT GRANIT STATES: nothing. copyrightText is EMPTY on both the CSD/RecreationResources service and on the Trails layer inside it, read live 2026-09-02, and an on-prem ArcGIS server carries no AGOL item-level licenseInfo either - the same genuinely-unstated position dec_licence records for DEC. WHAT CHANGED ON 2026-09-02: the maintainer authorised publication ('yes do publish these. Its publically available info.'), so this moved from 'unresolved' to 'maintainer_authorisation' the day it was registered. Public and queryable is not itself a reuse grant - that is SOURCE_SURVEY.md's rule and the reason the basis here is the maintainer's decision rather than GRANIT's terms. ONE THING THAT DISTINGUISHES THIS FROM THE FEDERAL CASE AND IS WORTH KNOWING BEFORE ANYONE RELIES ON IT: no public-domain-by-statute argument is available here. GRANIT is a university-run state clearinghouse that AGGREGATES contributed data - town, land-trust and agency layers, with its own ACCURACY column saying so - so the organization that could actually answer for a given segment may not be GRANIT at all. That makes this the thinner of the two authorisations even though it is the smaller dataset, and it is the one to revisit first if terms ever matter.

usfs_dispersed_camping_holdback._comment: WHY USFS's LARGEST SITE TYPE DOES NOT SHIP (#1207). 'CAMPING AREA' is 10,783 of usfs_rec_sites' 31,405 rows - bigger than CAMPGROUND (4,183) and GROUP CAMPGROUND (422) combined, and the single largest type in the layer. It is DISPERSED CAMPING, and this project has already decided not to publish that. THE EVIDENCE THAT IT IS DISPERSED, measured live 2026-09-02, because the type name alone does not say so. (1) development_scale reads 0 - undeveloped - on 8,135 of the 10,783, with 1,549 at scale 1 and 1,099 at scale 2. CAMPGROUND is the opposite shape: 3 on 2,490 rows, 4 on 960, 5 on 139, 2 on 594, and NOT ONE at 0 or 1. The two types do not overlap on the development scale at all. (2) The names are road references rather than places - 'FS1302-03', 'RD 614 SITE 13', 'RD 201 MI 8.2', 'LCR 839C-001', 'BRD21405-001', 'EAST FORK RESERVOIR RD-002' - which is what a catalogue of individual pull-offs along a forest road looks like, not a campground directory. THE DECISION THIS FOLLOWS IS NOT NEW. SOURCE_SURVEY.md section 3b holds back ATC's Campsite Sustainability Index for the same reason - 2,333 user-created campsites, 'publishing locations may be actively harmful', the ones land managers are often trying to close - and .claude/skills/pr-screenshot/SKILL.md names 'a dispersed or user-created campsite at a readable zoom' as one of four things that must never appear even in a SCREENSHOT, on the grounds that a map is a publication of coordinates. Shipping 10,783 of them as poi_type campsite would be that same publication at 4.6x the scale of the holdback that set the precedent, and it would arrive as a side effect of a change about the White Mountains rather than as a decision anybody took. WHAT WOULD REOPEN IT: the maintainer deciding that the Forest Service publishing these itself changes the argument - which is a real position, and different from ATC's case in that USFS is the land manager rather than a third party cataloguing what hikers made. That is a decision with an issue of its own, not a line in this one. THE MECHANICAL GUARD is export_nearby_poi.py's USFS_SITE_TYPES allowlist, which maps four types and no others.
